title: Forecasting: Time Series With ML & Foundation Models
subtitle: Why a random split flatters the model, the naive guess you must beat, lag features that turn forecasting into regression, where the model misses and how a safety buffer turns a forecast into a decision, and a foundation model that forecasts with no training

objectives.title: Validate Forecasts Honestly
objectives.description: TimeSeriesSplit and rolling-origin backtests: train on the past, test on the future, never the reverse. The 4%-offline-14%-live gap has one cause.

objectives.title: Turn Forecasting Into Regression
objectives.description: Lags, rolling means, calendar features, holidays — then any regressor you already know. Gradient boosting on lag features is the workhorse of industrial demand forecasting.

objectives.title: Beat the Baselines First
objectives.description: Seasonal naive, exponential smoothing, AutoARIMA via StatsForecast. If your model can't beat 'same hour last week,' it isn't a model.

objectives.title: Use a Foundation Model Zero-Shot
objectives.description: Chronos-2 and TimesFM forecast a series they have never seen, with no training. When they win, when they don't, and how to use one as the instant baseline.

agenda.title: Tomorrow's Morning Rush
agenda.description: Capital Bikeshare in Washington, DC: every night the vans get bikes ready for the 8 AM rush. Meet the data, 17,379 hours of real rentals with weather and calendar, the 165 missing hours (Hurricane Sandy), and three rhythms: daily, weekly, yearly.
bulletPoints: The rule of the game: forecast at midnight, for the next 24 hours

agenda.title: The Split That Sees the Future
agenda.description: Station 1, then the same gradient boosting model trained twice. A random split misses by about 25 rentals an hour, the honest time split by about 48: the random split looks 1.9 times better than the truth. Tomorrow has no neighbors from tomorrow.
bulletPoints: Rule 1: split by time, never shuffle
Test set: the last 8 weeks of 2012, Nov 6 to Dec 31

agenda.title: The Number to Beat
agenda.description: Station 2, then three naive guesses: same hour yesterday (63.5), same hour last week (72.5), the 7 day average (135). Yesterday wins because the test weeks hold Thanksgiving, Christmas and colder weather every week. Optional: MSTL from StatsForecast (59.4), and its limit: it only sees the series itself.
bulletPoints: Rule 3: a model only counts if it beats the naive baseline on the future
MAE in rentals per hour; no percentages when the series nears zero at 4 AM

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, guess tomorrow's 8 AM demand.

agenda.title: Forecasting as Regression: Lags + Gradient Boosting
agenda.description: Station 3, then the big idea: turn the past into columns (same hour yesterday, same hour last week, last week's average) and use gradient boosting from Session 7. TimeSeriesSplit for five pretend futures, then the real test: 39.1 against 63.5, 38 percent better.
bulletPoints: Rule 2: every column must be known at forecast time; rentals one hour before is a leak
Honest caveat: real weather stands in for a perfect weather forecast

agenda.title: Where It Misses, and the Decision
agenda.description: Errors by hour (8 AM is the hard hour), Thanksgiving week, and the Christmas Eve calendar lesson. Station 4, then forecast plus a safety buffer: short on 28 of 37 mornings with no buffer, 4 with 150 extra bikes, and the prices choose the buffer. Optional: Chronos-2 forecasts with no training, run live.
bulletPoints: A forecast is not a decision; forecast plus a buffer, priced by the cost of running short, is
A foundation model is the new first baseline

agenda.title: Your Turn & Project Check-In
agenda.description: Your Turn questions, then your project: does your data have a clock? Split by time in Milestone 3, name your naive baseline, and check every column against the moment of prediction.
bulletPoints: Milestone 4 slides on Canvas by 5:00 PM Mon Dec 7

activities.title: Beat Seasonal Naive: 24-Hour-Ahead Bike Demand
activities.description: Forecast hourly rentals one day ahead. Build the seasonal-naive baseline, then lag, rolling, and calendar features for HistGradientBoostingRegressor, validate with TimeSeriesSplit, and report MAE against the baseline — overall and by hour of day.

steps.title: Order and split by time
steps.description: Sort by time. The last 8 weeks (Nov 6 to Dec 31, 2012) are the test set; TimeSeriesSplit(5) on the rest. Never shuffle.

steps.title: Baseline
steps.description: Naive guesses: same hour yesterday and same hour last week. Compute MAE on the test weeks. The best one is the number to beat.

steps.title: Features knowable at forecast time
steps.description: lag_24, lag_168, the 7 day average ending 24 hours ago, hour, weekday, month, holiday, workingday, and the weather columns (standing in for a weather forecast).

steps.title: Model and diagnose
steps.description: HistGradientBoostingRegressor with early stopping. MAE overall, then groupby hour — where does the model still miss? Plot a test week: actual vs. baseline vs. model.

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

bikes = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harslan/isom-835/master/public/data/bike_hour.csv.gz')
bikes['ts'] = pd.to_datetime(bikes['dteday']) + pd.to_timedelta(bikes['hr'], unit='h')
bikes = bikes.set_index('ts').asfreq('h')              # one row per hour, gaps become empty rows
y = bikes['cnt'].interpolate()

X = pd.DataFrame({'hour': y.index.hour, 'weekday': y.index.dayofweek, 'month': y.index.month, 'year': y.index.year - 2011,
                  'holiday': bikes['holiday'].ffill(), 'workingday': bikes['workingday'].ffill(),
                  'temp': bikes['temp'].interpolate(), 'hum': bikes['hum'].interpolate(), 'weathersit': bikes['weathersit'].ffill(),
                  'lag_24': y.shift(24), 'lag_168': y.shift(168), 'avg_last_week': y.shift(24).rolling(168).mean()}).dropna()
y = y.loc[X.index]
past = X.index < '2012-11-06'                            # the last 8 weeks are the future

print(f"yesterday MAE: {mean_absolute_error(y[~past], X['lag_24'][~past]):.1f} rentals per hour")
gbm = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=2000, early_stopping=True, random_state=835).fit(X[past], y[past])
print(f"model MAE:     {mean_absolute_error(y[~past], gbm.predict(X[~past])):.1f} rentals per hour")

activities.discussionNote: The boosted model misses by about 39 rentals an hour against 64 for same hour yesterday. But look at the misses by hour and by day: 8 AM is the hard hour, and the worst days are Thanksgiving, Christmas and Christmas Eve, which the data does not even mark as a holiday. That is the honest story for the operations team: we are good on normal days, holidays need their own calendar, and the 8 AM buffer should be priced by the cost of running short.

takeaways.text: Split by time. A random split let the model copy neighboring days and looked 1.9 times better than the truth. TimeSeriesSplit and rolling origin backtests are the honest scoreboard.

Forecasting is regression on the past. Lag columns that respect the horizon, plus calendar and weather, let gradient boosting beat the best naive guess by 38 percent. Every column must be known at forecast time.
A forecast is not a decision. Forecast plus a safety buffer, chosen by the cost of running short, is. And a foundation model like Chronos-2 is the new first baseline: three lines, no training.
